Title: Uncontrolled Memory Allocation / Denial of Service in AtomicDoubleArray Deserialization (Android flavor)
Analysis:
This is the same vulnerability as found in the standard Guava package, but located in the Android-compatible flavor source code.

When deserializing an `AtomicDoubleArray` object from an untrusted source, the `readObject` method reads an integer `length` directly from the input stream. It then runs a loop `length` times, appending read values to an `ImmutableLongArray.Builder`. If an attacker provides a crafted serialized stream with a massive `length` value (e.g., `Integer.MAX_VALUE`), the loop will execute up to `length` times, and the `ImmutableLongArray.Builder` will iteratively grow its internal array, allocating massive amounts of memory. Although the loop will eventually throw an `EOFException` when the stream runs out of bytes, the JVM may exhaust its available heap memory or consume excessive CPU before that happens, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload:
Create a serialized stream of `AtomicDoubleArray` where the length field is overwritten to be `2147483647` (0x7FFFFFFF) but no actual double elements follow. When the target application deserializes this stream, it will parse the `length` of `2147483647` and attempt to build the `ImmutableLongArray`, crashing the JVM with an `OutOfMemoryError` or causing CPU starvation.

Title: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption in Collection Deserialization Helpers (Serialization.java - Android flavor)
Analysis:
The utility helper methods in `Serialization.java` (`populateMap`, `populateMultiset`, and `populateMultimap`) are used across various Guava collection classes (such as `HashMultiset`, `LinkedHashMultimap`, etc.) during custom deserialization (`readObject`). This file belongs to the Android-compatible flavor.

These helper methods read collection element sizes or entry counts (`size`, `distinctElements`, `distinctKeys`, and `valueCount`) from the `ObjectInputStream` and loop up to those counts to reconstruct the collections. 

Because there is no upper-bound validation on these integers before entering the loops or allocating collections/elements, an attacker can craft a serialized payload with massive count values. When deserialized, this triggers excessive loop execution and memory pre-allocation, leading to Out of Memory (OOM) errors or CPU exhaustion (Denial of Service).

### Conceptual Exploit Payload:
An attacker crafts a serialized payload representing a `HashMultiset` (or other Guava collection using these serialization helpers) where the `distinctElements` count is modified to a huge value (e.g. `1000000000`). Upon deserialization, `Serialization.populateMultiset` attempts to loop 1 billion times, reading objects from the stream and dynamically growing the underlying `HashMap`, causing the JVM to run out of memory or hang.

Title: Insecure Temporary Directory Creation on Windows due to Inherited ACLs
Analysis:
On Windows systems using Java versions prior to Java 17, when Guava creates a temporary directory using `Files.createTempDir()` or a temporary file using `FileBackedOutputStream`, it uses `JavaNioCreator` to create the resource securely. To do this, it specifies custom ACLs via the `userPermissions()` helper method (lines 167-194), which defines a single `ALLOW` entry for the current user.

However, on Windows, NTFS folders default to inheriting ACL permissions from their parent folders. Prior to Java 17, `java.nio.file.Files.createTempDirectory` and `Files.createTempFile` do not block ACL inheritance when creating a file/directory with custom attributes. As a result, the newly created temporary directory or file inherits the permissive ACLs of the parent directory (which is typically a shared temp folder like `C:\Windows\Temp` or `C:\Temp`). This means that other local users on the same machine can still read, write, or execute files inside the temporary folder, leading to Local Privilege Escalation, Information Disclosure, or local race condition attacks.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload:
1. A local attacker monitors a shared directory such as `C:\Windows\Temp`.
2. A privileged service running on the same machine under Guava calls `Files.createTempDir()` to write sensitive scripts or binary executable files.
3. The folder is created with the custom ACL but inherits the permissive parent directory's ACL (e.g. allowing `Authenticated Users` or `Everyone` read/write access).
4. The attacker accesses the folder, reads the sensitive files, or modifies/replaces binary files before they are executed, escalating privileges or stealing credentials.
